the analysis of the transcription regulation of pentose operons in gamma Proteobacteria and the development of computational methods for the identification of transcription regulatory elements.
the development of the comparative approach for the identification of transcription regulatory sites and the analysis of the pentose regulons of gamma proteobacteria.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

in gamma Proteobacteria, the transcription of the pentose utilization systems is controlled by the cAMP receptor-proteins, which bind in the regulatory regions to sites that are conserved among these genomes.
the transcription regulatory systems for the utilization of ribose, arabinose, and xylose are well conserved in gamma Proteobacteria.
the regulons and regulatory sites of the RbsR, AraC, and XylR regulators are conserved in the genomes of the gamma subdivision of the Proteobacteria.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the comparative approach to the identification of transcription regulatory sites in the genomes of related organisms is an efficient tool in genome-wide analyses of regulons and regulatory sites.
the comparative approach can be successfully applied for the identification of regulatory sites for the transcription regulators of pentose utilization in the gamma subdivision Proteobacteria.

the comparative analysis approach is a useful tool for the analysis of the regulatory networks of bacteria, and it may be used as a basis for the development of computational methods for the recognition of transcriptional regulatory sites.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the comparative approach is a powerful tool to identify new members of regulons, and to predict the function of operons that are regulated by a particular transcription regulator.
the analysis of the transcription regulatory networks of several closely related genomes can help identify regulatory sites in the genome of one of the species.
a comparative analysis of the regulons of related genomes allows one to detect regulatory sites and to identify new members of the regulon, and to predict the function of these new members.
